plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic drawing of a polarimeter, laid out as a single optical path running left to right in perspective. At the far left a lit incandescent bulb sits in a socket inside a yellow glow, labeled "Light source", and short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions emerge from it beneath the label "Unpolarized light". The beam is drawn as a flat pale yellow ribbon that passes through a circular disc with fine vertical striping, labeled "Polarizer", after which the red arrows all lie in a single vertical plane under the label "Polarized light". The ribbon then runs through a horizontal cylinder with a small filling stub on top, drawn with rounded ends and labeled "Sample tube containing organic molecules"; the red arrows inside progressively tip away from vertical as they move along the tube. Beyond the tube the beam meets a second striped disc labeled "Analyzer" and continues to the right, where a heavy red double-headed arrow lies at a slant. A vertical dashed reference line and a curved arrow mark the angle between the two, labeled with the Greek letter alpha, and a drawn eye at the right edge is labeled "Observer". Tracking one ribbon of light through every component makes the tilt of the arrows the quantity to follow. The arrangement shows how the rotation an optically active sample imposes on the plane of polarization is measured.

interactions.teaches: Rotating the scene reveals that each red arrow lies in a flat plane perpendicular to the beam, and that the polarizer, sample twist, and analyzer each redefine that plane in 3D

interactions.label: Sample rotation (deg)
interactions.teaches: The organic sample imposes a rotation: arrows inside the tube twist progressively from vertical at the entrance to this angle at the exit, and the emerging beam follows, so the observed rotation depends entirely on the sample's optical activity and sign

interactions.label: Analyzer angle (deg)
interactions.teaches: The observer rotates the analyzer until the tilted beam passes; when the analyzer plane equals the sample-imposed plane the measured alpha equals the sample rotation, showing how the rotation is read off the instrument

interactions.label: Send light pulse
interactions.teaches: A travelling pulse makes each component's role explicit: many-direction arrows collapse to one vertical plane at the polarizer, then progressively tilt through the sample tube, then emerge at the analyzer plane

demo_steps.title: Optically inactive sample
demo_steps.narration: With sample rotation 0 the arrows stay vertical through the tube and the analyzer at 0 passes full light; alpha reads 0.

demo_steps.title: Active sample, analyzer matched
demo_steps.narration: A +30° sample twists the arrows progressively; setting the analyzer to +30° aligns with the emerging beam so light passes and alpha = +30°.

demo_steps.title: Active sample, analyzer unmatched
demo_steps.narration: Leaving the analyzer at 0° while the beam emerges at +30° blocks most light, illustrating why the observer must rotate the analyzer to find the rotation.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Optical axis = +X (screen-right), beam travels left to right from x=0 to x=10. Bulb+socket at x≈0 with radial glow sprite (#ffee88). Unpolarized arrow cluster in the YZ plane at x≈1.2 (5-6 double-headed arrows at 0/45/90/135°). Polarizer disc at x≈2.5: CircleGeometry radius ~1.0 in YZ plane, grey rim #888888, vertical stripe fill #aaccbb. Polarized vertical arrow at x≈3.1. Sample tube: CylinderGeometry radius ~0.8, length ~3.0, axis along X from x≈3.6 to x≈6.6, light grey #cfd6d8 with rounded caps and a small vertical stub cylinder on top at x≈5.0. Inside-tube twist arrows: ~6 double-headed red (#cc1111) arrows at x = 3.8..6.4, each rotated about X by lerp(0, sampleRotation). Analyzer disc at x≈8.0, same style as polarizer but stripes rotate with analyzerAngle. Outgoing heavy red double-headed arrow at x≈9.0 rotated about X by analyzerAngle. Dashed vertical reference line (grey) and curved arc (black) at x≈9.5 spanning 0..analyzerAngle, label alpha. Eye sprite at x≈10.5. Beam ribbon: thin translucent box/plane #f5e6b8 opacity ~0.35 spanning the axis. World extents ~ X[0,11], Y[-1.5,2], Z[-1.5,1.5].
interactionPlan.notes: Build discs from CircleGeometry plus a CanvasTexture of parallel lines for the striping; rotate the analyzer's stripe texture and its outgoing arrow together about the X axis. Double-headed arrows = a thin cylinder shaft with two cone heads, grouped so a single rotation about X sets the polarization plane. The light pulse is a small emissive sphere lerped along +X; gate arrow-set emphasis by the pulse's x-region (unpolarized cluster bright before x=2.5, vertical arrow at polarizer, twisting arrows inside tube, outgoing arrow after analyzer). Recompute twist-arrow rotations and the alpha arc/label reactively on every slider change; show the alpha value as text. Keep both discs' stripe textures and all arrow groups in the scene and update transforms rather than rebuilding geometry.

authoredContext:
The angle of rotation can be measured with an instrument called a polarimeter, represented in the figure. A solution of optically active organic molecules is placed in a sample tube, plane-polarized light is passed through the tube, and rotation of the polarization plane occurs. The light then goes through a second polarizer called the analyzer. By rotating the analyzer until the light passes through it, we can find the new plane of polarization and can tell to what extent rotation has occurred.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Plane-polarized light passes through a solution of optically active molecules, which rotate the plane of polarization.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Unpolarized light from light source passes through polarizer, followed by polarized light, sample tube containing organic molecules, analyzer, and observer.

In addition to determining the extent of rotation, we can also find the direction. From the vantage point of the observer looking directly at the analyzer, some optically active molecules rotate polarized light to the left (counterclockwise) and are said to be levorotatory, whereas others rotate polarized light to the right (clockwise) and are said to be dextrorotatory. By convention, rotation to the left is given a minus sign (−) and rotation to the right is given a plus sign (+). (−)-Morphine, for example, is levorotatory, and (+)-sucrose is dextrorotatory.
